glossary.plain: A clear acrylic plastic (Plexiglas). BASS-II burned it as rods, slabs, films and a sphere section.
A cotton-fiberglass fabric used as a standard test fuel. The name comes from the earlier project it was made for.
glossary.quote: a composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (referred to as the SIBAL (Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speed) fabric)

glossary.plain: A fire-barrier fabric used widely on the ISS.
glossary.quote: it is heavily used aboard the International Space Station (ISS) as a fire barrier

glossary.plain: The potentiometer setting of the BASS-II fan: the knob that set the airflow. Airflow speeds on this site are converted from the fan's Air display reading with NASA's calibration (velocity = Air display × 1.0066 cm/s).
Air moving against the direction the flame spreads (the flame spreads upwind).
glossary.quote: Flames in microgravity are known to preferentially spread upwind (ie opposed flow), not downwind (i.e. concurrent flow)

glossary.plain: Air moving in the same direction the flame spreads (the flame spreads downwind), as in Earth's upward-burning Test 1.
glossary.quote: not downwind (i.e. concurrent flow) as in the normal gravity upward flammability screening Test 1

glossary.plain: Air flowing straight at the end of a rod, so the flame sits on the rod's tip like a cap.
glossary.quote: Microgravity Flammability Boundary for Polymethylmethacrylate Rods In Axial Stagnation Flow

glossary.plain: A flame going out because the airflow is too weak to feed it.
glossary.quote: Quenching extinction occurs at very low forced flows, where the flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue flame and oscillates with increasing amplitude just before going out.

glossary.plain: A flame going out because the airflow is too strong.
glossary.quote: Blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.

glossary.plain: Small separate flames that a starved flame front breaks into; each burns its own channel toward the incoming air.
glossary.quote: the flame breaks into numerous “flamelets” that form a Turing-type reaction-diffusion fingering pattern as they spread across the fuel

glossary.plain: The Microgravity Science Glovebox, the sealed workspace on the ISS where BASS and BASS-II burned their samples.
glossary.quote: MSG Microgravity Science Glovebox, a facility aboard ISS

points.quantity: Flame tip spread rate (4 mm rod)

luci_notes: Flown on Blue Origin New Shepard on 4 February 2025; vehicle spin at 11 RPM gave simulated lunar gravity at a 1.22 m radius.
Two samples burned in air at normal pressure: SIBAL fabric (5 cm x 30 cm) and a 4 mm diameter PMMA rod.
The 1 g SIBAL flame went out about 45 seconds sooner than the lunar-g flame.
The PMMA rod spread about 6 cm before extinction at lunar g; steady spread was not reached.
Burns lasted more than two and a half minutes. Two camera views show the Coriolis force pulling the PMMA flame away from the rod's axis.

statements.text: On the NASA KC-135 aircraft, thin cellulose samples (1, 2 and 4 cm wide) burned upward in air at 0.2-0.4 atm at 0.10 g, 0.16 g (lunar) and 0.38 g (martian). Steady spread speeds and pyrolysis lengths were approximately proportional to the gravity level.
For a cellulose fuel in opposed flow, the limiting oxygen index on Earth is 16.5% O2, but with flow on the order of spacecraft ventilation (5-20 cm/s) flames can be sustained at 14% O2.
Plastic cylinders burned aboard Mir did not spread along the rod as intended; the flame stabilized at the front tip of the rod and burned like a candle flame at the end of a fat wick.
Flames in microgravity preferentially spread upwind (opposed flow), not downwind as in the normal-gravity upward screening Test 1.

Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested lunar gravity could be more hazardous, since flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks there; related work suggests the oxygen concentration needed for flammability reaches a minimum near lunar gravity.

Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2), planned for launch in late 2026, will burn four solid fuel samples in quiescent habitable atmospheres in real lunar gravity, with cameras, radiometers and an oxygen sensor.

Near extinction, in weakly convective environments such as microgravity or in vertically confined spaces, a flame breaks into numerous flamelets that form a fingering pattern as they spread across the fuel. This extends the flammability range to lower opposed flow velocities, lower oxygen concentrations or higher heat loss.
statements.where: p. 1 (NASA ground experiment in a narrow flow channel)

statements.text: US spacecraft crews turn off ventilation to help put out a fire, then reactivate it to clear the smoke. Some flamelets can survive, and NASA Glenn experiments demonstrated that flamelets quickly grow into a large fire when ventilation increases.
Partial-gravity test times: about 5 s in drop towers, about 25 s aboard aircraft, and about 150 s on a spinning sounding rocket.

flamelet_figure.caption: Top: at the end of the test, the airflow is increased to see if the flamelets can be blown out. Instead, they flare up and remerge into a full flame front. Bottom: green light reveals the black char fingers left on the paper once the flame broke into flamelets. Air came from the top; at 2 cm/s past the sample the flamelet population was about 13.
flamelet_figure.setting: NASA Glenn ground experiment: a narrow flow channel that suppresses buoyancy, simulating microgravity. Not flight data.
